content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers fair representation as a bi-level optimization problem where the data representation is first learned then the fair predictors are optimized based on this fixed representation. A theoretical analysis on the the error gap of the implicit algorithm is conducted, and some positive results have been shown in the paper. The paper presents an interesting and topical problem and is easy to follow.
content.main_review:
-- Lacks proper motivation. The paper first motives this work by stating learning a fair representation with respect to the sufficient rule is necessary and appealing for the specific real-world intelligence system designing which is a universal motivation applicable for most of the fairness studies. The computational complexity of gradient-descent directions is later discussed but there is no experimental results to support this claim.   

-- The paper is not self-contained. Some key terms such as the sufficient rule and sufficient gap are not well covered.  

-- My other concern is that whether the positive results obtained can be generalized to other setups: if the sensitive attribute is highly associated with the class label, the learned data representation for overall loss purpose will be naturally highly associated with the sensitive attribute. Then the subsequent 'fair' predictors learned based on this fixed representation are not guaranteed. A correlation analysis might be of helpful for justification purpose. One relevant question is that whether the dataset is divided into subgroups based on the sensitive attribute for fair predictors training? If so, how about the potential information loss?  

-- Some baselines from adding fairness constraints during the training process are considered. However, fundamental ones such as the "Learning fair representations" work is not compared against although discussed in the related work. In addition, non deep learning approaches such as fairness-aware decision trees enjoy low computationally and memory complexity, which is one motivation of this work, in comparison to deep learning methods, are ignored. Can the proposed method outperform these efficient fair models when the complexity is higher? Otherwise the merit of this approach is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting problem. However, the concerns is that the paper lacks proper motivation. The paper also lacks sufficient justification of the proposed method.

content.title: Thanks for your review [1/2]
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful and thoughtful reviews! We have revised our paper based on your comments. Below are our responses to your questions.
 
--------------
1. **Motivation and complexity**
 
> a fair representation with respect to the sufficient rule is necessary and appealing for the specific real-world intelligence system designing which is a universal motivation applicable for most of the fairness studies
 
Thanks for your remark. Below are our summaries of motivations.

- *Sufficiency rule is important in practice and fair learning*
 
Health systems rely on commercial algorithms for identifying patients with complex health needs. In their essence, these algorithm outputs a healthcare need score $\hat{Y}=t$, where a higher score indicates a sicker patient with more critical healthcare needs.
(Obereyer et al. 2019, Science) revealed that a widely used algorithm, typical of this industry-wide approach and affecting millions of patients, exhibits significant racial bias. Indeed, for a given predicted healthcare need score ($\hat{Y}=t$), black patients are in fact considerably more sick than white patients ($E_{black}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] > E_{white}[Y|\hat{Y}=t]$). Remedying this disparity would require to increase the percentage of black patients receiving additional healthcare from 17.7 to 46.5% (Obereyer et al. 2019).
Therefore, to address this bias is equivalent to enforce the sufficiency rule, such that $E_{black}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] = E_{white}[Y|\hat{Y}=t]$.

From the algorithmic perspective, according to (Barocas, 2019), the widely adopted fair criteria such as *independence* and *separation* are generally not compatible with the *sufficiency rule*. Based on these, we think it is important to develop novel fair approaches w.r.t. the *sufficiency rule* because of the practical and algorithmic demands.

- *Why fair deep representation learning?*
 
The learned fair representation can easily transfer the unbiased prior knowledge to the downstream tasks. For example, in NLP, fair embedding can provide both useful and unbiased representation for different goals (translation, sentiment analysis, etc.). The additional comparison and discussion with the non-deep method are delegated in Q4.

> The computational complexity of gradient-descent directions is later discussed but there are no experimental results to support this claim.
 
Below we provide the computational and memory complexity analysis of gradient estimation w.r.t. $\lambda$, (i.e, $grad(\lambda)$), based on (Shaban et al., 2018):
 
| Method | Time complexity | Memory complexity |
|------|-----|---------|
| (T-step) Explicit| $TC$ | $2TM$|
| Implicit| $C + S$ | $2M$ |


 where $T$ is the iteration step in the inner-loop optimization, $C$ is the time complexity in computing the Hessian matrix $\nabla_{\lambda}\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}$, $S$ is the computational complexity for the conjugate gradient solver and $M$ = memory($\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}(h,\lambda)$) is the space complexity of the partial gradient. The implicit approach analytically shows its efficiency when the inner-optimization step increases.
 
From the empirical aspect, we visualized the computational time between the implicit and explicit approaches, shown in Appendix D.2 (Fig. 9, Page 17) in the paper. The experimental results also verify the efficiency of the implicit approach.  

2.  **Definition of sufficiency rule and sufficiency gap**

> Some key terms such as the sufficient rule and sufficient gap are not well covered.
 
We appreciate your feedback and we have carefully revised the paper (adding Section 2 Preliminaries with explainations) for a clear illustration. Below is a brief introduction.  

We denote X as the input, $Y\in\mathcal{Y}$ as the label and $\hat{Y}\in\mathcal{Y}$ as the output of the predictor. We consider binary sensitive attributes (two subgroups) with distribution $D_0$ and $D_1$.

- *Sufficiency rule* is defined as:
 
$$E_{D_0}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] = E_{D_1}[Y|\hat{Y}=t],~~\forall t\in\mathcal{Y}.$$
 
Since our paper addresses classification and regression problem simultaneously, we discuss the sufficiency gap in these two scenarios, respectively.
 
- *Sufficiency gap* in binary classification is defined as:

$$ \Delta Suf_{C} =\sum_{y\in\{-1,1\}}|D_0 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y) - D_1 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y)|.$$
  
- *Sufficiency gap* in regression ($Y\in R$) is defined as:

$$ \Delta Suf_{R} =  \int_{t} |D_0 (Y\leq t|\hat{Y} \leq t) - D_1 (Y \leq t |\hat{Y} \leq t)| dt.$$

content.title: Thanks for your review [2/2]
content.comment:
3. **Correlation analysis**
 
> if the sensitive attribute is highly associated with the class label, the learned data representation for overall loss purpose will be naturally highly associated with the sensitive attribute. Then the subsequent 'fair' predictors learned based on this fixed representation are not guaranteed. A correlation analysis might be of helpful for justification purpose.
 
Thanks for your remark. We computed Pearson correlation coefficients between the sensitive attribute $A\in\{0,1\}$ and the label $Y$ in our datasets.
 
| Toxic-Comment | CelebA| Law | NLSY |
|------|---------|-----|---------|
|0.30| -0.35 |0.18 | -0.29 |

The results suggest the weak correlation between $A$ and $Y$, where fair learning is possible.

> One relevant question is that whether the dataset is divided into subgroups based on the sensitive attribute for fair predictors training? If so, how about the potential information loss.
 
The data is divided into two subgroups but the information is generally not lost during the training. Intuitively, all the subgroups pass through the *same* representation function and the optimal predictor is encouraged to be invariant.
From a theoretical perspective, the subgroups can be viewed as different tasks (i.e, multi-task learning), then the prediction performance can be better than simply training the whole dataset if the shared information is properly learned.

4. **Comparison with non-deep approaches**
 
> non deep learning approaches such as fairness-aware decision trees enjoy low computationally and memory complexity, which is one motivation of this work, in comparison to deep learning methods, are ignored
 
- *Comparison with fairness-aware decision tree*
 
We compare with FAHT (implemented by Java) (Zhang et al. IJCAI 2019) in the Toxic classification task and included a brief discussion in the paper (Appendix D.3, Table 5). Below are our results

| Method | Accuracy (larger is better) | $\Delta$Suf_C (smaller is better) | 
|------|---------|-----|
|FAHT| 0.596 |0.397 |
|Implicit (ours)|0.760|0.051|

The better results of the implicit method may come from two aspects: (1) the Toxic task is a relative high-dimensional classification problem ($X\in\mathbb{R}^{748}$), where the deep learning-based approach is more effective in handling the high-dim dataset. (2) The FAHT aims to minimize the statistical parity (the *independence rule*), which is **not** compatible with the *sufficiency rule*. According to the analysis of (Barocas, 2019), when the sensitive attribute (A) and label (Y) are not independent (as justified by the Pearson correlation coefficient in Q3), the *sufficiency* and *independence* cannot both hold.
 
- *The implicit approach aims to reduce the complexity in bi-level optimization of **learning fair deep representation learning** .*
 
As for the non-deep learning methods, it is generally difficult to learn a good representation for many real-world applications. For example, we conducted the computer vision task (CelebA, Sec 6.2.2) in the paper, which contains ~100K real images with resolutions 178×218. It is *highly difficult* to learn the representation in such a case by using the conventional non-deep model. In contrast, our goal is to improve the training efficiency (time and memory) in learning fairness w.r.t. the deep models (e.g., ResNet18).

-----

We are grateful again for your insightful comments. We hope our responses can address your main concerns on *motivations* (why sufficiency and fair-representation learning, validation of computational complexity) and *justifications* (the correlation study, comparison with non-deep, benefits of deep learning in the computer vision). We are also quite happy to provide additional information for the possible further questions.
 
References

* Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Ziad Obermeyer, Brian Powers, Christine Vogeli, Sendhil Mullainathan. Science 2019.
* Racial Bias in Pulse Oximetry Measurement. Michael W. Sjoding, Robert P. Dickson, Theodore J. Iwashyna, Steven E. Gay, Thomas S. Valley. N Engl J Med 2020.
* Truncated Back-propagation for Bilevel Optimization. Amirreza Shaban, Ching-An Cheng, Nathan Hatch, Byron Boots. AIStats 2019
* FAHT: An Adaptive Fairness-aware Decision Tree Classifier. Wenbin Zhang,
and Eirini Ntoutsi. IJCAI 2019.

content.title: About the applicability
content.comment:
> So do you know your work can be applicable when the sensitive attribute is highly associated with the class label? How if so?

Thanks for your excellent question. If we understand this question correctly, the applicability means whether the proposed idea can keep good prediction performance and fairness (under sufficiency rule) when sensitive attribute (A) and label (Y) are highly correlated.

**Response** The proposed idea can work when $A$ and $Y$ are highly correlated but **only in the specific scenarios**. Below we consider a simple synthetic example for the illustration.

We consider binary attribute $A$ and input $X$ containing two features $X=(X_b,X_c)$ and binary label $Y\in 0,1$. Concretly, $X_c$ is the content feature with $X_c \in 0,1$ and $X_b$ is the background feature with $X_b \in 0,1$. We further assume that 
- Only the content feature $X_c$ decides the label $Y$ (i.e, $X_c=0, Y=0$; $X_c=1,Y=1$);
- The senstive attribute $A$ decides the background feature $X_b$.

Based on the assumptions, we generate the following two subgroups

In $A=0$, 
$$P(X_b=0, X_c=0, Y=0) = 0.97$$

$$P(X_b=0, X_c=1, Y=1) = 0.01$$

$$P(X_b=1, X_c=0, Y=0) = 0.01$$

$$P(X_b=1, X_c=1, Y=1) = 0.01$$


In $A=1$

$$P(X_b=1, X_c=1, Y=1) = 0.97$$

$$P(X_b=1, X_c=0, Y=0) = 0.01$$

$$P(X_b=0, X_c=0, Y=0) = 0.01$$

$$P(X_b=0, X_c=1, Y=1) = 0.01$$

Then we can compute the **$A$ is highly correlated with $Y$** (The Pearson correlation coefficient between $A$ and $Y$ is $0.96$). $A$ is also highly correlated with background feature $X_b$.  

If we adopt our idea in learning invariant and optimal predictors, thus we have the predictor $\hat{Y}=X_c$ (i.e, the content feature), since $X_c$ is invariant w.r.t $A$ and can achieve optimal risk on the different subgroup. Then we can compute the accuracy and Sufficiency gap in this scenario, by using the following confusion matrix.

|$A=0$|$\hat{Y}=0$  | $\hat{Y}=1$ |  
|-------|--------|---------|
|$Y=0$|0.98| 0|
|$Y=1$| 0| 0.02 |

|$A=1$|$\hat{Y}=0$  | $\hat{Y}=1$ |  
|-------|--------|---------|
|$Y=0$|0.02| 0|
|$Y=1$| 0| 0.98 |

- (*Accuracy and Sufficiency rule can both hold in this scenario*) We can compute the average accuracy on two groups are 100\% and Sufficiency gap $\frac{1}{2}\sum_y|D_0(Y=y|\hat{Y}=y)-D_1(Y=y|\hat{Y}=y)| = |\frac{0.98}{0.98+0}-\frac{0.02}{0.02+0}|$ is zero. 

    Interestingly, we can compute the Demographic Parity (DP, Indenpendecy rule) if $\hat{Y}=X_c$, i.e, $|D_0(\hat{Y}=1)-D_1(\hat{Y}=1)|=0.96$, which suggests a quite large value. The reason is that the sensitive attribute $A$ and the label $Y$ are highly correlated then Independence and Sufficiency rule cannot simultaneously hold. 

In contrast, if we adopt the background feature $X_b$ as the predictor $\hat{Y}=X_b$, which does not meet our principle since *it is not the optimal predictor on both subgroup*. We can also compute the confusion matrix on these two sub-groups

|$A=0$|$\hat{Y}=0$  | $\hat{Y}=1$ |  
|-------|--------|---------|
|$Y=0$|0.97| 0.01|
|$Y=1$| 0.01| 0.01 |

|$A=1$|$\hat{Y}=0$  | $\hat{Y}=1$ |  
|-------|--------|---------|
|$Y=0$|0.01| 0.01|
|$Y=1$|0.01| 0.97 |

The corresponding accuracy is still high with $0.98$. However, the Sufficiency gap can be around $0.49$ ($|\frac{0.97}{0.97+0.01}-\frac{0.01}{0.01+0.01}|\approx 0.49$), which suggests a considerable unfair predictor w.r.t. the Sufficiency rule.


As for discovering the general assumptions and theoretical understandings, we think it is a promising and interesting research topic, which can be left as future work by further exploring [1-2].

Reference 

[1] Causal inference using invariant prediction: identification and confidence intervals. Jonas Peters, Peter Buhlmann and Nicolai Meinshausen

[2] Invariance, Causality and Robustness. Peter Buhlmann


-----------
Thanks again for your insightful comments! We hope our response can address your question.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the learning of fair representations (and classifiers). In particular, the paper considers the (group) sufficiency rule for fairness and optimization path alignment to achieve the fairness requirement. The paper considers a representation fair if the optimization path (gradient steps) of subgroups are equivalent / invariant, with respect to optimal subgroup classifiers. To this end, the paper introduces a bi-level optimization problem for a representation function, which is solved by approximating gradients with the implicit function theorem. The approximation error of the gradients and the convergence of representation function (appendix) are analysed. Their algorithm is then experimentally tested under various datasets and compared to various baseline approaches.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
  - The proposed path optimization framework of fairness is intuitively easy to understand.
  - Optimization of the proposed bi-level optimization problem has a clear connection to group sufficiency + predictive parity (Prop. 1).
  - The implicit path algorithm is well motivated through the implicit function theorem approximation of the gradient.
  - The experimental section is extensive and shows promising results.
  - Very well presented with useful figures.

Weaknesses:
  - A majority of the paper considers approximate versions of the classifiers $ h^{\varepsilon}_{i} $. However, the fairness proposition (Prop. 1) requires optimal classifiers and also requires each subgroup classifier to be equal. How does the proposition adapt when these assumption break? In particular, is there a way to relax the assumption to give approximate predictive parity fairness?
  - Time taken in the experiments could be documented to compare approaches.
  - It would be useful to clarify the limitation / cost of considering sensitive attributes beyond the binary case.
  - Discussion about the link between the complexity of classifiers $ h $ and the changes of accuracy / fairness would be interesting. For example, in the CelebA dataset a two layer neural network was used (in contrast to the other dataset which use a linear predictor). Do you achieve similar results with just a single layer?
  - In the experiments, did the representations change much from the original representations? I.e., did you observe some type of Lipschitz condition on learnt $ \lambda $.

Minor:
  - Typo on Figure 1, red loss gradient should have subscript "1".
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I would recommend an accept for the paper. Although I have a few questions regarding Prop 1 / fairness when considering more relaxed assumptions, the paper provides a nice intuitive framework and theoretically well motivated algorithm. Furthermore, the extensive experiments show that the proposed algorithm has promise when considering group sufficiency fairness.

content.title: Thanks for your review
content.comment:
Thanks for your thoughtful reviews! Based on your comments, we have revised our paper accordingly. Below are our responses to your questions.

> A majority of the paper considers approximate versions of the classifiers
 
Thanks for your remark. We have revised the paper to clarify *h* as the predictor can be either binary-classifier or regressor, the proposed algorithm applies for both settings.

> the fairness proposition (Prop. 1) requires optimal classifiers and also requires each subgroup classifier to be equal. How does the proposition adapt when these assumption break? In particular, is there a way to relax the assumption to give approximate predictive parity fairness?
 
Thanks for your comments. Proposition 1 is based on the original bi-level loss

$$\min_{\lambda} \mathcal{L}_0(h_0^\star,\lambda) + \mathcal{L}_1(h_1^\star,\lambda) $$

$$s.t. h^\star_0 = h^\star_1,  h^\star_0 \in argmin_h \mathcal{L}_0(h,\lambda), h^\star_1 \in argmin_h \mathcal{L}_1(h,\lambda)$$

In practice, we reformulate the bi-level loss via the Lagrangian relaxation by introducing the fair coefficient $\kappa > 0$.

$$\min_{\lambda} \mathcal{L}_0(h_0^\star,\lambda) + \mathcal{L}_1(h_1^\star,\lambda) + \frac{\kappa}{2}||h_0^\star-h_1^\star||_2^2 $$

$$s.t. h^\star_0 \in argmin_h \mathcal{L}_0(h,\lambda), h^\star_1 \in argmin_h \mathcal{L}_1(h,\lambda)$$

where the fair constraints are actually controlled by $\kappa$. i.e, A larger $\kappa$ encourages stronger constraints on the optimal invariant predictor (shown in Fig.1,2). 

> Time taken in the experiments could be documented to compare approaches.
 
Thanks for your comment. To show the efficiency of the implicit approach, we empirically compare the time complexity between the explicit and implicit approach (Appendix D.2, Fig.9). The results reveal the computational efficiency of the implicit approach when the inner-level optimization iteration is large.

> It would be useful to clarify the limitation / cost of considering sensitive attributes beyond the binary case

Thanks for your suggestion. We think it is practically feasible to extend to discrete protected features with distributions $D_1,\dots, D_N$. For example, the bi-level objective can be naturally extended as:

$$ \min_{\lambda}\sum_n \mathcal{L}_{n}(h_n^\star,\lambda)+\sum_n \sum_m \frac{\kappa_n^m}{2}||h_n^\star-h_m^\star||_2^2$$

$$ s.t. h^\star_{n} \in argmin_{h} \mathcal{L}_{n}(h,\lambda) $$

Where $(n,m)\in[1, N]$ is the pair of the sensitive attributes.  Compared with the binary group, we introduce the pair-wise regularization ($||h^\star_n-h^\star_m||$) term to ensure the invariance between each pair of the sensitive attributes $(n,m)$. However, determining the coefficient $\kappa_n^m$ will become practically challenging since the hyperparameter space is much larger (O($N^2$)) than the binary case.

If the sensitive attribute is purely continuous, we think a simple empirical approach is to cluster the continuous attribute into several discrete groups, then conducting the pairwise optimization.

> For example, in the CelebA dataset a two layer neural network was used (in contrast to the other dataset which use a linear predictor). Do you achieve similar results with just a single layer?
 
Thanks for your comments. We conduct an additional ablation study in changing the layers in CelebA dataset (one layer and three layers). Below are our results.
 
|  | Accuracy (larger is better) | $\Delta$Suf_C (smaller is better) | 
|------|------|------|
|One layer| 0.776 |0.063 |
|Two layers|0.794|0.074|
|Three layers|0.800|0.069|
 

We observed the two and three layers predictors can improve the accuracy since the non-linear activation function improves the expressive power of the neural network. The results in three layers indicate similar results to the two layers predictor, in terms of accuracy and fairness.

> In the experiments, did the representations change much from the original representations? I.e., did you observe some type of Lipschitz condition on learnt $\lambda$.
 
We visualized the gradient norm of the representation $\lambda$ i.e, $||\text{grad}(\lambda)||$ in the training. (Appendix D.2, Fig.10, Page 18). We observe that $||\text{grad}(\lambda)||$ convergences to zero in the training.     
 
---------------
 
We are grateful again for your all insightful comments! We are also quite happy to provide additional information for the possible further questions.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers the fair representation learning problem. In particular, the fairness notion utilized is (close to) the sufficient rule, and this paper proposes a bi-level implicit path alignment algorithm to (approximately) achieve it.

The contribution of the paper includes (1) an empirical algorithm for DNN to (approximately) achieve the sufficient rule, (2) theoretical analysis w.r.t. effectiveness of the algorithm as well as its application scope (classification and regression).
content.main_review:
Overall, the paper is relatively well-written. It would be greatly appreciated if the authors can kindly clarify the following questions/comments:

### q1: the exact characterization of the term "invariant"

I understand that (as indicated by the paper) one of the primary goals of finding fair representation is to clear the way for downstream tasks.
While I am not questioning intuition, I found the characterization of the term "invariant" in the paper is a little bit confusing. In particular, at the very beginning of Page 2, it was mentioned that "the optimal predictor learnt on the embedding space [is] invariant from sub-groups", which according to my understanding is saying that the downstream predictor $h$ is irrelevant to the value of the protected feature; on Page 3 (the paragraph **Learning Invariance**) the word "invariance" is used to describe the OOD behaviour of the learnt representation, i.e., w.r.t. the embedding function $\lambda$. Which kind of invariance exactly is the one readers should focus on? (or both?)

### q2: potential extension to cases where the protected feature is non-binary

From the setting and the theoretical results, it is clearly presented that the discussion is limited to the binary protected feature scenarios. I am just wondering can we naturally extend the proposed framework to non-binary protected feature cases (e.g., the ratio of people of certain demographic backgrounds in the community is a continuous variable)? If such extension is highly nontrivial (which I suspect so), what is the biggest impediment (theoretical or empirical or both)? Including such a discussion would be very helpful in order to understand the practical significance of the proposed approach.

### q3: regarding the "implicit path alignment"

To the best of my knowledge, using implicit path alignment w.r.t. downstream predictor is novel in the fair representation learning literature. I have a question regarding the way it is implemented. As indicated in the first equation on Page 4, the paper considers the t-th update (instead of the whole path), but in the experimental setting, it is mentioned that the algorithm encourages the "identical one-step optimization path". I personally find this a bit confusing. If we were to keep each one-step optimization identical, is it explicit path alignment instead of implicit?

content.title: Thanks for your review
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful and constructive reviews! Based on your comments, we have revised our paper accordingly. Below are our responses to your questions.

1. the exact characterization of the term "invariant"
> characterization of the term "invariant" in the paper is a little bit confusing.... at the very beginning of Page 2, it was mentioned that "the optimal predictor learnt on the embedding space [is] invariant from sub-groups..
downstream predictor H is irrelevant to the value of the protected feature..
on Page 3 (the paragraph Learning Invariance) the word "invariance" is used to describe the OOD behaviour of the learnt representation, i.e., w.r.t. the embedding function λ.
 
We appreciate your thoughtful comment! In our paper, the term "invariant" refers to the *invariant optimal* predictor that is trained on the top of data representation w.r.t. different subgroups. (Inner-Loop in the bi-level optimization).
We have revised the related work for a clear illustration. 

2. potential extension to cases where the protected feature is non-binary
> can we naturally extend the proposed framework to non-binary protected feature cases (e.g., the ratio of people of certain demographic backgrounds in the community is a continuous variable)? If such extension is highly nontrivial (which I suspect so), what is the biggest impediment (theoretical or empirical or both)?

Thanks for your suggestion. We think it is possible to extend to discrete protected features with distribution $D_1,\dots,D_N$. For example, the bi-level objective can be naturally formulated as 

$$ \min_{\lambda}\sum_n \mathcal{L}_{n}(h_n^\star,\lambda)+\sum_n \sum_m \frac{\kappa_n^m}{2}||h_n^\star-h_m^\star||_2^2$$

$$ s.t. h^\star_{n} \in argmin_{h} \mathcal{L}_{n}(h,\lambda) $$

Where $(n,m)\in[1, N]$ is the pair of the sensitive attributes.  Compared with the binary group, we introduce the pair-wise regularization ($||h^\star_n-h^\star_m||$) term to ensure the invariance between each pair of the sensitive attributes $(n,m)$. However, determining the coefficient $\kappa_n^m$ will become practically challenging since the hyperparameter space is much larger (O($N^2$)) than the binary case.

If the sensitive attribute is indeed a real value, we think a simple practical approach is to *cluster the continuous attribute into several discrete groups*, then conduct the pair-wise bi-level optimization. At the same time, there may be difficulty in measuring fairness. E.g, if the sensitive attribute is the ratio of people of certain demographic backgrounds, the corresponding sufficiency gap will be hard to estimate, since current metrics are defined on the discrete sensitive attribute.

3. regarding the "implicit path alignment"

> As indicated in the first equation on Page 4, the paper considers the t-th update (instead of the whole path), but in the experimental setting, it is mentioned that the algorithm encourages the "identical one-step optimization path". I personally find this a bit confusing. If we were to keep each one-step optimization identical, is it explicit path alignment instead of implicit?

Thanks for your remark. The "identical one-step optimization path" in the experimental part refers to the one-step approach, which is proposed as the baseline to compare the implicit approach. Specifically, one-step alignment is viewed as a special case of explicit path alignment. It assumes that $h_0^\star \approx h^0 - \nabla_{h_0} \mathcal{L}_0(h_0,\lambda)$ 

and $h_1^\star \approx h^0 - \nabla_{h_1} \mathcal{L}_1(h_1,\lambda)$.  i.e, the optimal predictor is obtained from *only one step gradient-descent* in the inner-loop. 

Then we have the $||\nabla_{h_0} \mathcal{L}_0(h_0,\lambda)-$
 
$\nabla_{h_1} \mathcal{L}_1(h_1,\lambda)||_2^2$ as the regularization term.

---------------
We are grateful again for your all insightful comments! We hope the explanations can address your confusions. We are also quite happy to provide additional information for the possible further questions.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a methodology for fair representation learning.
The core novelty of the proposal is the satisfaction of a sufficient rule.
Experimental results claim good performance with respect to other approaches in terms of an accuracy-fairness tradeoff, in which a sufficient gap is measured.
content.main_review:
The core weakness of this paper is in terms of presentation. The writing lacks self-sufficiency, while it also contains language errors that confuse the reader.
The core concepts of sufficient rule, sufficiency, and sufficient gap are brought up several times, but never adequately defined.

The closest we come to an intuitive statement is this statement:
"the sufficient rule is encouraged, which reflects the same likelihood of recidivism irrespective of the individual’s group membership"
It is not defined what "reflects" means in the above, and the rule, as explained, is not connected to a mathematical definition.
Then, the concept is invoked in a mathematical manner in Proposition 1. However, even there, the concept of sufficiency is invoked, but left undefined.
Eventually, in Section 5.1, we see a definition of the sufficient gap, which is claimed to recover a predictive parity gap.
However, both concepts are left without a discussion of the intuition and semantics underlying them.

Due to the above gaps, the main claim of the paper to demonstrate that "the bi-level objective is to fulfil the sufficient rule" is left shaky.

content.title: Thanks for your review [1/2]
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments! We are sorry if some points of the paper appear not to be clearly explained. Based on your feedback, we have carefully revised our manuscript by (1) clarifying the fairness notation and providing intuitions, and (2) adding Sec 2 for introducing the related definitions.

Throughout our paper, we introduced two concepts: the *sufficiency rule*, and the *sufficiency gap* for classification and regression. Below are the definitions and explanations.

1. **Sufficiency rule**
 
Based on (Barocas 2019; Liu 2019), we denote $X$ as the input, $Y\in\mathcal{Y}$ as the label, and $\hat{Y}\in\mathcal{Y}$ as the output of the predictor. We consider binary sensitive attributes (two subgroups) with distribution $D_0$ and $D_1$. The sufficiency rule is defined as:

$$E_{D_0}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] = E_{D_1}[Y|\hat{Y}=t],~~\forall t\in\mathcal{Y}$$

Based on the aforementioned definition, Proposition 1 demonstrated the bi-level objective is fulfilling the sufficiency rule.

2. **Why sufficiency rule is important in real-world application and fair learning?**

Health systems rely on commercial algorithms for identifying patients with complex health needs. In their essence, the algorithm outputs a healthcare need score $\hat{Y}=t$, where a higher score indicates a sicker patient with more critical healthcare needs.
(Obereyer et al. 2019, Science) revealed that a widely used algorithm, typical of this industry-wide approach and affecting millions of patients, exhibits significant racial bias. Indeed, for a given predicted healthcare need score ($\hat{Y}=t$), black patients are in fact considerably more sick than white patients  ($E_{black}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] > E_{white}[Y|\hat{Y}=t]$). Remedying this disparity would require increasing the percentage of black patients receiving additional healthcare from 17.7 to 46.5% (Obereyer et al. 2019).
Therefore, addressing this bias is equivalent to enforce the sufficiency rule, such that $E_{black}[Y|\hat{Y}=t] = E_{white}[Y|\hat{Y}=t]$.

From an algorithmic perspective, according to (Barocas, 2019), the widely adopted fair criteria such as *independence* and *separation* are generally not compatible with the *sufficiency rule*. Based on these, we think it is important to develop novel fair approaches w.r.t. the sufficiency rule because of the practical and algorithmic demands.

3. **Sufficiency gap in binary classification** is defined as:

$$\Delta Suf_{C} =\sum_{y\in\{-1,1\}}|D_0 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y) - D_1 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y)|.$$

**Intuition:**  $\Delta Suf_{C}$ encourages having two subgroups with identical Positive Predicted Value (PPV) and identical Negative Predicted Value (NPV). On the practical side, considering that the healthcare evaluation system outputs either High Risk or Low Risk. (Obermeyer et al., Science 2019) essentially revealed that $D_{\text{black}}(Y=\text{High Risk}|\hat{Y}=\text{Low Risk}) > D_{\text{white}}(Y=\text{High Risk}|\hat{Y}=\text{Low Risk})$ -- the severity of black patients condition is actually underestimated. 

If $\Delta Suf_{C}$ is small, such a racial discrimination can be remedied. (based on the fact of binary classification $D_{\text{black}}(Y=\text{High Risk}|\hat{Y}=\text{Low Risk})+D_{\text{black}}(Y=\text{Low Risk}|\hat{Y}=\text{Low Risk}) = 1$)

4. **Sufficiency Gap in regression** is defined as:

$$ \Delta Suf_{R} =  \int_{t\in\mathcal{Y}} |D_0 (Y\leq t|\hat{Y} \leq t) - D_1 (Y \leq t |\hat{Y} \leq t)| dt$$

**Explanation:** $\Delta \text{Suf}_{C}\in[0,1]$ is an approximation of $|D_0 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y) - D_1 (Y=y|\hat{Y}=y)|, \forall y\in \mathbb{R}$, since the latter is difficult to estimate in regression.
 
**Intuition:** We assume the health system outputs a *real-value* healthcare score $\hat{Y}=t$ (a higher score indicates a more sick person, that requires more healthcare), then the aforementioned example that suggests $D_{black} (Y >  t|\hat{Y} \leq t) > D_{white} (Y > t |\hat{Y} \leq t)$. i.e, for the patients whose predicted healthcare score is less than $t$, the actual proportion of sicker ($Y>t$) in black patients is considerably higher than white patients.

This racial bias is also revealed in the application of medical devices such as Pulse Oximetry Measurement (Sjoding et al., N Engl J Med 2020), where black patients had nearly three times the frequency of occult hypoxemia that was not detected by pulse oximetry ($D(Y > t|\hat{Y}\leq t)$) as white patients. Therefore a smaller $\Delta\text{Suf}_{R}$ suggests a better prediction disparity.
 
---------
We are grateful again for your feedback and comments. We hope these explanations and intuitions can address the points of confusion you raised. We have carefully revised the paper based on the aforementioned elements. We are also quite happy to provide additional information for further possible questions.
